## Overview
This dataset contains EEG data collected while Japanese native speakers read Japanese newspaper articles from the Balanced Corpus of Contemporary Written Japanese (BCCWJ; Maekawa et al., 2014). Stimuli were presented word by word. This dataset is part of BCCWJ-Brain, This dataset is part of BCCWJ-Brain; three types of brain data (fMRI, MEG, and EEG) were acquired from separate groups of participants using the same stimuli, enabling cross-modality comparisons of language processing with high spatial and temporal resolution respectively.
The BCCWJ-Brain collection consists of the following datasets:

- BCCWJ-fMRI: ds007752 ([https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007752](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007752))
- BCCWJ-MEG: ds007763 ([https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007763](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007763))
- BCCWJ-EEG: ds007753 ([https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007753](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007753))


## Participants
Data from forty-one participants were included in the dataset (22 females and 19 males; mean age=20.5 (SD = 2.89)). All participants were right-handed, had no neurological illness, and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. 

## Data Acquisition
EEG data were recorded using a BrainAmp amplifier (Brain Products GmbH, Germany) with a 64-channel electrode cap. The online reference electrode was placed at FCz, and the ground electrode was placed at AFz. An electrode was placed below the right eye (IO) to monitor ocular artifacts. Electrode impedances were kept below 20kΩ prior to the recording. Data were recorded at a sampling rate of 1,000Hz.

## Experiment Procedure
Twenty Japanese newspaper articles were used as stimuli. Stimuli were presented word by word using rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) implemented in PsychoPy (Peirce, 2007, 2009). Each stimulus was presented for 500 ms, followed by a 500 ms blank screen. The order of the newspaper articles were randomized.

## Event Timing
The presentation trigger was **accidentally** sent at each word's **offset** rather than its onset (an unintended error in the stimulus-presentation script). Because each word was displayed for a fixed 500 ms, the true onset is 500 ms before the recorded trigger. This is represented in the standard BIDS way: in ``events.tsv`` the ``onset`` column is the true word onset (relative to the first EEG data point) and the ``duration`` column is 0.5 s (the display duration), so the recorded trigger corresponds to ``onset + duration``. The raw ``.eeg/.vhdr/.vmrk`` markers are left exactly as recorded (at the offset). The **derivatives are onset-corrected**: the word markers in the continuous ``*_raw.fif`` and the evoked ``*_reref0.1-40-ica_ave.fif`` are time-locked to word onset, so a continuous derivative can be epoched directly (e.g., window −100 to 1000 ms, baseline −100 to 0 ms). In dataset version 1.0.0 the ``events.tsv`` ``onset`` column actually held the offset times and the derivatives sat at the offset; both were corrected in version 2.0.0 (see ``CHANGES`` and the code repository at [https://github.com/osekilab/BCCWJ-Brain](https://github.com/osekilab/BCCWJ-Brain)).

## Data Preprocessing
EEG data were preprocessed using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; Gramfort et al., 2013) and
Eelbrain (v0.40.3; Brodbeck et al., 2023). The data were read with an easycap-M1
electrode layout and one bipolar EOG channel (IO). Independent component analysis
(ICA) was fitted on a 1–40 Hz bandpass-filtered copy of the continuous data
(components explaining 99% of the variance), and components reflecting ocular
artifacts were identified and removed. The resulting decomposition was applied to
the separately 0.1–40 Hz bandpass-filtered data, which was then re-referenced to
the common average. All three continuous derivatives keep the recorded 1,000 Hz
sampling rate.

For the evoked derivative, the preprocessed data were segmented into epochs from
−100 to 1,000 ms relative to word onset, baseline-corrected on the −100 to 0 ms
pre-stimulus interval, and decimated by a factor of 5 (every 5th sample, an
effective 200 Hz; no anti-aliasing filter is required because the signal is
already low-passed at 40 Hz). Artifact-contaminated epochs were rejected using
Eelbrain's epoch selection with a 150 µV peak-to-peak threshold, so the number of
averaged epochs varies across participants (983–1,640 of the 1,642 word events;
mean 1,544). 

```
derivatives/
└── sub-XX/
    └── eeg/
        ├── sub-XX_task-BCCWJreading_eeg_raw.fif                  (converted to FIF, unfiltered, 1,000 Hz)
        ├── sub-XX_task-BCCWJreading_eeg_0.1-40_raw.fif           (0.1–40 Hz bandpass, 1,000 Hz)
        ├── sub-XX_task-BCCWJreading_eeg_reref0.1-40-ica_raw.fif  (+ ICA + average reference, 1,000 Hz)
        └── sub-XX_task-BCCWJreading_eeg_reref0.1-40-ica_ave.fif  (evoked, word-onset locked, 200 Hz)
```

## Code
Analysis and validation code for the BCCWJ-Brain datasets — including the grand-average ERP script (`EEG_grand_average.py`), which also shows how to build onset-locked epochs from the continuous derivatives — is available on GitHub: [https://github.com/osekilab/BCCWJ-Brain](https://github.com/osekilab/BCCWJ-Brain).

## Notes
Since the BCCWJ texts are not copyright-free, texts for the experiment is not included in this dataset. To obtain the text, users must register for access to BCCWJ ([https://bccwj-data.ninjal.ac.jp/](https://bccwj-data.ninjal.ac.jp/)) separately.  See [https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp/bccwj/en/subscription.html](https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp/bccwj/en/subscription.html) for the details. Once access is granted, we provide a script to incorporate the text into the corresponding ``events.tsv`` files.
